Case A · oracle-assisted token-ahead prefetch

ShadowKV with one-token-ahead prediction

Official model configs feed a GenZ roofline model, the generated performance bundle is read through LLMServingSim, and ShadowKV selection/offload is added as explicit per-block events. The page estimates TTFT, TPOT, output throughput, and simultaneous-user capacity without downloading model weights.

1–2 nodes · 8×A800 80 GB each PP8×TP2 / TP8 / dual TP4 72K / 128K / 256K input Official HF weights → BF16 compute 1.56% KV selection BF16 exact-KV storage Oracle: 80% recall / 80% precision 60% temporal-cache reuse GenZ core profile · A100-measured hardware envelope

Official-weight placement

Safetensor totals come from the official Hugging Face repositories. Stored weights are unpacked or converted inside fused kernels; BF16 activations and BF16 tensor-core compute are assumed, without retaining a full BF16 copy.

Kimi Code 2.7 595.2 GB INT4 · two nodes

The files technically occupy 93% of one node's nominal HBM, leaving too little runtime workspace. The estimate therefore uses eight contiguous TP2 stages—roughly 7–8 layers each—with four stages on each server.

GLM-5.3 755.6 GB FP8 · two nodes

The official checkpoint cannot fit in 640 GB. Eight contiguous TP2 stages—roughly 9–10 layers each—avoid expert all-to-all across IB; FP8 weights are converted to BF16 fragments as consumed.

GLM-5.3-Flash 328.3 GB FP8 · one node

One TP8 replica occupies about 41.0 GB/GPU. Its 34 linear-attention layers keep recurrent state in HBM; only 11 sparse-attention layers enter the ShadowKV cache path.

DeepSeek V4 Flash 159.6 GB FP4/FP8 · one node

Two independent four-GPU replicas remain feasible. Mixed-format weights are converted in the matmul path and never expanded into a persistent BF16 model image.

Topology assumption: Kimi and GLM use PP8×TP2. Stages 1–4 are on server A and stages 5–8 on server B, so only one BF16 activation crosses 400 Gb/s IB. GLM-5.3-Flash uses TP8 on one node; DeepSeek V4 Flash uses two independent TP4 replicas. Cross-node expert parallelism is excluded.

FP8 KV-storage overlay

Exact/offloaded KV and the selected GPU working set use E4M3 plus one FP32 scale per 128 values. Attention still computes in FP16/BF16 after fused dequantization.

Bytes About 48.4% less KV traffic

One FP8 byte plus scale metadata costs about 1.031 bytes/value, versus 2 bytes/value for BF16. The cache representation in HBM nearly halves.

Ampere conversion Conversion is not free

A custom A100-SXM4 SM80 kernel measured 455 Gvalue/s for fused E4M3 block-scale conversion to BF16. The trace uses that center and samples 320–520 Gvalue/s; an unfused PyTorch cast-plus-scale path measured only about 80 Gvalue/s.

Admission HBM sets the memory-only ceiling

FP8 KV shrinks the HBM cache representation. System RAM is unbounded; the first whole request beyond the HBM maximum is rejected.

What the pure-TP case says

Decode Concurrency becomes practical

Only 1.56% of the exact cache is consumed per decode step. Overlapped prefetch reduces exposed transfer time, while pure TP replicates the selected latent rows on every rank and therefore limits capacity more than the earlier context-sharded assumption.

Prefill TTFT remains the bottleneck

ShadowKV does not remove the compute needed to process 128K or 256K prompts. A simultaneous cold-start burst can therefore wait minutes even when later token streaming is acceptable.

Pipeline Eight request groups fill PP8

A lone decoder still traverses all eight stages. With enough known requests, the scheduler chooses a small microbatch and overlaps up to eight successive decode iterations; the slowest generated stage sets cadence.

Assumptions

“Perfect condition” means flawless execution of the stated design—not a magical oracle. The central advisory oracle has 80% recall and 80% precision and is verified by current-token landmark selection.

Hardware and runtime

  • Each node has 8× NVIDIA A800 80 GB, approximately 640 GB nominal aggregate HBM; Kimi and GLM consume two IB-connected nodes, while GLM Flash and V4 Flash consume one.
  • An A100-SXM4 proxy measured about 22.0 GB/s long-transfer H2D to one GPU but only 25.4 GB/s aggregate when both GPUs in a TP2 stage copied concurrently. The model enforces both ceilings, plus a still-assumed 180 GB/s node host-DRAM ceiling.
  • 400 Gb/s InfiniBand is modeled as approximately 40 GB/s usable one-way payload bandwidth. Stages 1–4 are on server A and 5–8 on server B, so pipeline parallelism crosses IB once per forward pass.
  • System-RAM capacity is treated as unbounded for admission. The default is pure TP with decode-context parallel degree 1: MLA/latent history, sparse-index rows, and ShadowKV's latent-derived state are replicated on every TP rank. PP still assigns disjoint layer ranges.
  • Each TP rank directly DMA-loads its replicated selected latent rows. A load-once-then-NVLink-broadcast runtime could reduce host traffic, but is not assumed without an implementation measurement.
  • Custom serving code, optimized kernels, static knowledge of all requests, and one model deployment at a time.

Model and cache behavior

  • Official Hugging Face storage formats are retained: Kimi native INT4, GLM and GLM Flash FP8 with documented BF16 exclusions, and V4 Flash mixed FP4/FP8. Fused kernels dequantize into registers/shared memory and compute in BF16; no persistent BF16 weight copy is allocated.
  • Exactly 1.56% of context entries are selected: 1,152 at 72K, 2,048 at 128K, and 4,096 at 256K.
  • Temporal reuse is one-token set overlap: 60% of the entries needed by the current token are assumed to remain in the GPU sparse buffer from the preceding token. Over the other 40%, 80% recall means the oracle fetches 80% of the truly needed entries early, while 80% precision means only 80% of everything it prefetches is useful. For 100 selected entries, that is 60 resident, 32 correctly prefetched, 8 unnecessarily prefetched, and 8 fetched just in time.
  • The current query still runs landmark selection to verify the required set and discover oracle misses. Only prefetch and reconstruction that finish before their consumer are hidden.
  • Every cache-bearing transformer block is charged separately, following ShadowKV Table 13's causal order: select → max(reconstruct K, fetch V) → sparse attention.
  • FP8 selected-cache conversion is charged once at sparse-attention consumption for the entire selected set—including reused and full-resident rows—not again in miss materialization.
  • The ShadowKV overlay conservatively retains trained native sparse-index state: GLM/GLM Flash use 132-byte FP8-plus-scale rows and V4 uses the reference 256-byte BF16 row. ShadowKV selector timing acts as the selection proxy; a second index kernel is not added.
  • GLM-Flash's fixed KDA state is charged as FP32 recurrent matrices plus BF16 convolution buffers and is head-sharded across TP8. Its decode update uses a separate state-read/write and arithmetic roofline lower bound.
  • No quality degradation from sparse selection and no pathological attention pattern that defeats the predictor.
Simulation boundary: GenZ supplies operator roofline timing; its generated per_sequence.csv bundles are loaded by LLMServingSim's production interpolation path. LLMServingSim also supplies vLLM-compatible PP partitioning. This repository adds ShadowKV events externally because stock tiered-KV recall does not represent landmark selection or low-rank key reconstruction.
Memory-accounting correction: the previous published revision divided latent/cache bytes by TP degree. These graphs retire that shortcut. Pure TP at DCP1 replicates MLA/latent history, native index rows, ShadowKV state, and direct H2D payload on every rank; only query-head arithmetic and GLM-Flash KDA head state retain TP sharding. Explicit DCP needs its own communication model.

Why the models differ

The same 1.56% policy interacts with four substantially different attention/cache designs.

Kimi Code 2.7

Largest decode-side upside

Its dense MLA-style long-context attention has the largest cache-side opportunity. The generated core curve is fast at one sequence, while PP8 microbatching reuses weights without collapsing the pipeline to one large batch. At the OOM boundary, aggregate throughput can be high while per-user latency is poor.

Capacity model: the exact CPU cache is unbounded for admission. HBM counts the rank-160 key factors, chunk-8 landmarks, sparse exact-value buffer, native non-overlaid state, official-format weights, and a 6 GiB/GPU runtime reserve.

72K HBM max116 users
128K HBM max65 users
256K HBM max33 users
GLM-5.3

Capacity gain more than TPOT gain

GLM already uses a sparse attention indexer. Its 755.6 GB FP8 checkpoint requires two nodes and leaves less per-GPU cache headroom than Kimi. The enlarged memory-only batches are therefore capacity points, not acceptable latency targets.

Capacity model: the ShadowKV representation and the checkpoint's trained 132-byte DSA index rows are retained in HBM while the exact CPU cache is excluded from admission. Bandwidth for fetching the replicated latent rows remains in the latency model.

72K HBM max60 users
128K HBM max34 users
256K HBM max17 users
GLM-5.3-Flash

Hybrid attention changes the cache problem

The official 320B/18B-active model mixes 34 KDA linear-attention layers with 11 sparse-attention layers. The 11 growing MLA histories and index rows replicate across TP8; the fixed KDA recurrent and convolution state is charged separately and remains head-sharded.

Capacity model: only the 11 sparse layers receive the ShadowKV representation. Linear-attention recurrent and convolution states remain device-resident and are included in HBM admission; projection weights stay in the GenZ core while recurrent updates use a separate lower-bound roofline.

72K HBM max69 users
128K HBM max40 users
256K HBM max20 users
DeepSeek V4 Flash

Least incremental ShadowKV benefit

Its native compressed/sparse cache is already smaller than the adapted ShadowKV representation. Two four-GPU replicas give the highest aggregate rate, and the native no-ShadowKV case consequently admits more users at the same HBM boundary.

Capacity model: ShadowKV overlays only the ratio-4 portion; ratio-128/local-window state and the BF16 index rows retain their reference representation and native-attention cost. Because V4 is already compressed, this overlay consumes more HBM than its native cache in this model.

Method and interpretation

How the displayed metrics are derived

per-user throughput = aggregate output throughput ÷ active requests TPOT (ms/token) = 1000 ÷ per-user throughput average burst TTFT ≈ pipeline-aware single-prompt TTFT × (requests per replica + 1) ÷ 2 average 512-token completion = average TTFT + 511 × TPOT

For Kimi and GLM, the single-prompt center includes chunked PP8 overlap during prefill; they each remain one logical model replica. Decode cannot pipeline successive tokens from one user because of the autoregressive dependency. DeepSeek V4 Flash has two TP4 replicas; GLM Flash has one TP8 replica. The scheduler prioritizes first tokens.

Metric definitions

TTFT
Time from admission until the first generated token, including prompt prefill and queueing inside the closed burst.
TPOT
Steady-state time between generated tokens after prefill.
Total tok/s
Tokens produced by the entire model deployment across all active requests—two nodes for Kimi/GLM, or one node for GLM Flash/V4 Flash.
Per-user tok/s
Fair-share generation rate for one continuously decoding request.
mb
Selected microbatch size: concurrent sequences in one PP request group, or the local continuous batch for a PP=1 replica.
100% load
One closed batch at the case-specific HBM OOM boundary—not stable 100% arrival-rate utilization. In every case, system RAM is unbounded for admission and the next request that does not fit HBM is rejected.
Queueing warning: at sustained 100% offered utilization, mean queue delay has no finite bound. A real service needs admission control, prompt-length-aware scheduling, and reserved prefill capacity even if every request is known in advance.

The run used two idle A100-SXM4-80GB GPUs on the same NUMA node, a locked Pixi environment on local NVMe, PyTorch 2.9.1 with CUDA 12.9, pinned host buffers, and repeated CUDA-event timings. The committed result omits the private hostname and GPU UUIDs.

For one PP8×TP2 stage with per-GPU payload \(B_g\), the transfer floor is now

\[ t_{\mathrm{H2D,stage}}=\max\!\left( \frac{B_g}{22.0\ \mathrm{GB/s}}, \frac{2B_g}{25.4\ \mathrm{GB/s}}, \frac{2B_g}{180\ \mathrm{GB/s}} \right). \]

The second term is the measured topology correction: two simultaneous copies do not receive \(2\times22.0\) GB/s. Other TP2 pairs are assumed independent until the node host-DRAM ceiling, because only one pair was available for this run.

The fused FP8 kernel sustained about 1.38 TB/s of useful input, scale, and BF16-output traffic. A separate unfused PyTorch cast-plus-scale path measured about 80 Gvalue/s, so fusion is a required success condition, not a cosmetic optimization.

How the calibration is used: GenZ receives 312 TFLOP/s BF16 peak, a 40% compute-efficiency prior, the 1,765 GB/s streaming ceiling, and a kernel-memory efficiency chosen so the effective model-weight bandwidth equals 51.6% of the 2,039 GB/s A100 nameplate. FP8 conversion uses the measured 455 Gvalue/s center. This grounds a roofline, but it still does not reproduce real fused frontier-model kernels, routing imbalance, framework gaps, or a measured TP8 collective.

Detailed estimation model

The expandable derivation makes every major scaling assumption explicit and separates calculated quantities from calibrated performance estimates.

Show the mathematical model and model-specific reasoningOfficial weight bytes, PP8×TP2, selection, pipeline bubbles, PCIe/IB traffic, throughput, TTFT, and queueing

1. Sparse working-set size

Let \(N\) be the prompt length, \(\alpha=0.015625=1/64\) the selected fraction, \(L_p\) the number of cache-bearing layers on pipeline stage \(p\), \(d_c\) the exact cached latent width, and \(q\) the main-cache bytes/value: 2 for BF16 or 1.03125 for FP8 plus scales. The selected entries per decode token are

\[ S(N)=\lceil\alpha N\rceil, \qquad S(131{,}072)=2{,}048, \qquad S(262{,}144)=4{,}096. \]

With pure TP and decode-context parallel degree 1, every TP rank receives a full copy of the selected latent rows for its stage:

\[ B_{\mathrm{sel,GPU},p}(N)=S(N)L_pd_cq, \qquad B_{\mathrm{sel,TP\ group},p}=G_sB_{\mathrm{sel,GPU},p}. \]

2. Oracle recall, precision, reuse, and PCIe traffic

Let \(S_t\) be the exact entries selected for the current token and \(H_{t-1}\) the entries retained in the GPU sparse buffer after the preceding token. Temporal reuse is the fraction of the current required set that is already resident, \(r=|S_t\cap H_{t-1}|/|S_t|=0.60\). This is one-step working-set overlap—not shared-prefix reuse and not 60% of the full context.

The oracle predicts only among the required entries that are not already resident. If \(M_t=S_t\setminus H_{t-1}\) is that miss set and \(P_t\) is the set prefetched one token ahead, then

\[ R_o=\frac{|P_t\cap M_t|}{|M_t|}=0.80, \qquad P_o=\frac{|P_t\cap M_t|}{|P_t|}=0.80. \]

Recall measures how much of the true miss set was covered early; precision measures how much speculative traffic was useful. These definitions separate useful coverage from false-positive traffic:

\[ B_{\mathrm{prefetch}}=(1-r)\frac{R_o}{P_o}B_{\mathrm{sel}}=0.40B_{\mathrm{sel}}, \qquad B_{\mathrm{JIT}}=(1-r)(1-R_o)B_{\mathrm{sel}}=0.08B_{\mathrm{sel}}. \]
Worked example: 100 entries in the final selected set
State or eventEntriesInterpretation
Temporal-cache hit60Already resident; no host-to-device transfer
True non-resident miss set40The entries that actually need materialization
Correct early prefetch3280% recall over the 40 required misses
False-positive prefetch832 useful entries are 80% of 40 total prefetched entries
Just-in-time fetch8The 20% of true misses not covered by the oracle

The host transfers 40 entries speculatively plus 8 just in time: 48 entries in total. With perfect overlap, only the 8 just-in-time entries block the current token. Fetch-at-decode would transfer only the 40 true misses, but all 40 would be exposed on the critical path. Because the selected set itself is 1.5625% of context, the 48 transferred entry-equivalents are 0.75% of the full context.

The total newly materialized traffic is 0.48× the selected set, versus 0.40× for fetch-at-decode with the same reuse. Prefetch is allowed to overlap the preceding token, but the selector and the 0.08× just-in-time miss set remain on the current token's critical path. The measured proxy provides about 22.0 GB/s to one GPU and 25.4 GB/s aggregate to both TP2 GPUs, so

\[ t_{\mathrm{JIT,TP2}}\approx\max\!\left( \frac{B_{\mathrm{JIT,GPU}}}{22.0\ \mathrm{GB/s}}, \frac{2B_{\mathrm{JIT,GPU}}}{25.4\ \mathrm{GB/s}} \right). \]
BF16 worked example: offloaded exact cache path\(L\)\(d_c\)\(B_{\mathrm{sel}}\)/GPU at 128K / 256K\(t_{\mathrm{JIT}}\) at 128K / 256K

GLM main latent, busiest PP8×TP2 stage1057622.5 / 45.0 MiB0.15 / 0.30 ms

The table is a BF16 transfer example. In FP8 mode its byte and link-time columns multiply by \(1.03125/2\); conversion of the complete selected set is charged once in the later sparse-attention roof.

Provenance matters: the 60% central value is adapted from ShadowKV's reported roughly 60% chunk hit rate/temporal locality. The assumed oracle recall and oracle precision are both 80%; these are hypothetical values for this report's proposed token-ahead predictor, not measurements reported by ShadowKV or validated on these frontier models. A perfect authoritative oracle would use \(R_o=P_o=1\) and could make verification optional. This page instead keeps landmark selection on the critical path to verify the advisory oracle.

3. ShadowKV HBM footprint and OOM admission

Host capacity is intentionally unbounded, so exact offloaded KV never limits admission. H2D and host-DRAM bandwidth remain finite latency constraints. The HBM boundary explicitly counts ShadowKV's rank-160 key factors, chunk-8 landmarks, and exact sparse buffer. For one overlaid layer, let \(r_k=160\), \(c=8\), \(S=\lceil N/64\rceil\), \(O=24\lfloor S/1024\rfloor\), and

\[ n_L=\max\!\left(0,\left\lfloor\frac{N}{c}\right\rfloor-4-O\right), \qquad n_B=S+128+c(O+4). \]

With cached width \(d_c\), the modeled HBM values in an offloaded layer are

\[ V_{\mathrm{shadow,layer}} =Nr_k+r_kd_c+n_Ld_c+n_Bd_c. \]

The four terms are the low-rank \(U\), low-rank \(SV\), landmarks, and sparse selected/outlier/local buffer. A full-resident layer instead uses \(Nd_c+n_Ld_c\). Native layers outside the overlay—for example V4 Flash ratio-128/local state—retain their official growing representation.

Layer count is explicit. For main-cache bytes/value \(q\), overlaid layers \(\mathcal L_{S,p}\), native non-overlaid layers \(\mathcal L_{N,p}\), native index states \(\mathcal I_p\) with row size \(e_i\), and TP-sharded fixed KDA state \(F_p/G_s\), the per-request allocation that controls OOM is

\[ K_{\mathrm{GPU}}(q)=\max_p\!\left\{ q\!\left[ \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_{S,p}}V_{\mathrm{shadow},\ell} +\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal L_{N,p}}V_{\mathrm{native},\ell} \right] +\sum_{i\in\mathcal I_p}n_i e_i+\frac{F_p}{G_s} \right\}. \]

The displayed results use pure TP/DCP1. Main MLA/latent history, native index rows, and ShadowKV's latent-derived state are replicated per TP rank; only the fixed KDA head state uses the \(1/G_s\) factor. GLM index entries are always 132 bytes, while the V4 reference index entries are 256-byte BF16 rows, independent of the main-cache toggle.

For the most heavily loaded stage GPU, official-format weight footprint \(W_{\mathrm{GPU}}\), replica count \(R\), and per-request cache footprint \(K_{\mathrm{GPU}}\), the common admission rule for all three cases is

\[ H_{\mathrm{GPU}}=0.90(80\ \mathrm{GiB})-W_{\mathrm{GPU}}-6\ \mathrm{GiB}, \qquad C_{\max}=R\left\lfloor\frac{H_{\mathrm{GPU}}}{K_{\mathrm{GPU}}}\right\rfloor. \]

The first whole request beyond \(C_{\max}\) is rejected. The 90% setting is the configured HBM allocation boundary, so “OOM boundary” here means the report's planning OOM limit rather than consuming every physical byte.

\(W_{\mathrm{GPU}}\) balances the checkpoint's total stored bytes evenly over the GPUs in one replica; it is not a stage-specific packed-weight manifest. Cache bytes use the busiest PP stage, so uneven real weight placement can shift the Kimi/GLM whole-request boundary by a few requests. Final deployment admission should substitute measured per-stage allocations.

Resulting BF16 / FP8 ShadowKV admission ceilings

At 72K/128K/256K: Kimi is 116/65/33 versus 226/127/64; GLM is 60/34/17 versus 109/61/31; GLM Flash is 69/40/20 versus 123/71/36; and V4 Flash is 72/40/20 versus 128/72/36. Each pair is BF16-main-cache versus FP8-main-cache. These are memory-feasible maxima, not independently optimized SLO limits.

Worked layer-accounting check: Kimi 128K FP8

The busiest PP8 stage contains eight of Kimi's 61 layers. Under pure TP, native cache is \(8\times131{,}072\times576\times1.03125/2^{30}\approx0.5801\) GiB/request/GPU, giving \(\lfloor31.35/0.5801\rfloor=54\) users. The modeled ShadowKV representation is 0.2456 GiB/request/GPU, giving 127 users. There is no division by TP2; explicit DCP2 would be a different communication model.

Full-model geometry is checked before placement. At 256K with BF16 main cache, one logical sequence is 17.15625 GiB for Kimi, 22.61426 GiB for GLM including its fixed-format index, and 2.97610 GiB for GLM Flash including pooled index and fixed KDA state. PP assigns layer subsets to stages; pure TP then replicates each stage's MLA/index portion.

4. GenZ core profile, LLMServingSim bridge, and throughput

For every aggregate operator \(j\), GenZ evaluates the roofline below. Arithmetic is BF16; \(b_j\) is the official stored weight precision, and conversion occurs while the weight tile is consumed:

\[ t_j=\max\!\left( \frac{F_j}{\eta_C P_{\mathrm{BF16}}}, \frac{B_{a,j}+B_{w,j}(b_j)+B_{o,j}}{\eta_M BW_{\mathrm{HBM}}}, \frac{W_j}{R_{\mathrm{dequant}}} \right). \]

The central inputs are \(P_{\mathrm{BF16}}=312\) TFLOP/s, \(\eta_C=0.40\), effective model-weight bandwidth \(0.516\times2039=1052\) GB/s, and \(R_{\mathrm{dequant}}=455\) Gvalue/s. Quantized conversion is treated as fused and overlapping; an unfused implementation would add, rather than maximize, the conversion term.

MoE weight traffic is batch-dependent. Under the documented balanced-routing assumption, \(C\) sequences making \(k\) expert choices among \(E\) experts touch an expected

\[ E_{\mathrm{active}}(C)=E\left[1-\left(1-\frac{1}{E}\right)^{kC}\right]. \]

This is why the generated Kimi/GLM core curve rises with batch size: weight reuse in shared projections is offset by an expanding set of expert matrices. The deterministic 1–4,096 sequence sweep contains both total-core and stage-core rows in LLMServingSim-compatible per_sequence.csv; the estimator calls LLMServingSim's own interpolation function for every stage.

For every cache-bearing block \(\ell\), the external extension emits selection, background prefetch, miss materialization, sparse attention, and optional fused FP8 KV conversion. The causal critical path is

\[ t_{\ell}=t_{\mathrm{select},\ell} +\max(t_{K,\ell},t_{V,\ell}) +t_{\mathrm{attention},\ell}, \]

Here \(t_{\mathrm{attention}}\) is the maximum of the scaled Table-13 memory center, direct TP-sharded BF16 arithmetic, and—only for FP8—the full selected-set conversion roof. Conversion is not added again to miss materialization. The Table-13 center scales with measured HBM bandwidth and no uncited launch floor is inserted.

For microbatch size \(b\), \(g=\lceil C/b\rceil\) request groups, and stage service \(s_p(b)\) including local ShadowKV work, native attention for non-overlaid V4 layers, the GLM-Flash KDA state-update roof, and the outgoing PP edge, the steady recurrence is

\[ T_{\mathrm{step}}(C,b)=\max\!\left[ \max(P,g)\max_p s_p(b),\ g\,t_{\mathrm{prefetch,node}}(b) \right], \qquad b^*=\arg\min_{1\le b\le\lceil C/P\rceil}T_{\mathrm{step}}(C,b). \]

The total and fair-share output rates then follow directly:

\[ Y_{\mathrm{total}}(C,N)=\frac{1000C}{T_{\mathrm{step}}(C,N)}, \qquad Y_{\mathrm{user}}(C,N)=\frac{1000}{T_{\mathrm{step}}(C,N)}, \qquad \mathrm{TPOT}=\frac{1000}{Y_{\mathrm{user}}}\ \mathrm{ms}. \]

ShadowKV Table 13 reports three separate per-transformer-block terms at 24×128K: selection of \(0.58+0.07+0.15=0.80\) ms, materialization of \(\max(1.36,1.66)=1.66\) ms, and sparse attention of 0.21 ms. Attention is not hidden inside materialization: its measured memory roof is scaled by selected rows and the custom joint-latent width, then roofed against TP-sharded BF16 arithmetic and FP8 conversion. This assumes a custom fused latent cache path; Kimi's literal Transformers implementation expands per-head K/V and would be materially larger. These terms are multiplied by every cache-bearing block. A deterministic 256-sample sensitivity run varies GenZ compute/memory efficiency, dequant throughput, PCIe, host DRAM, NVLink payload, selector timing, and materialization timing; its p10–p90 range is a parameter-sensitivity interval, not a confidence interval.

5. Model-specific calibration logic

Kimi Code 2.7

Dense long-context attention makes \(B_{\mathrm{HBM}}\) large. The native-INT4 checkpoint uses 595.2 GB before runtime allocations, so it is split across two nodes. PP8 needs eight independent request groups for full occupancy; the search keeps at least eight groups and balances MoE reuse against stage cadence.

GLM-5.3

Its native sparse indexer already reduces attention work. The 755.6 GB FP8 checkpoint must span two nodes. Each PP stage reads a generated service-time row; the scheduler overlaps request groups up to PP depth while the expert-occupancy model penalizes oversized microbatches.

GLM-5.3-Flash

The official config defines 45 layers: 34 KDA linear-attention and 11 DSA layers. Only the 11 DSA layers receive ShadowKV events. The linear recurrent state remains in HBM. Its 328.3 GB checkpoint fits one node only with TP8, so small TP collectives form a visible part of the core floor.

DeepSeek V4 Flash

The trained compressed/sparse cache already makes \(B_{\mathrm{HBM}}\) small. Its 159.6 GB mixed FP4/FP8 checkpoint permits two four-GPU replicas; official stored bytes and fused conversion are represented directly in the GenZ operator roofs.

6. Cold-start TTFT

Let \(T_0(N)\) be the estimated single-request prefill time and let \(R\) be the number of model replicas. For a simultaneous closed burst of \(C\) requests, balanced across replicas, define

\[ c_r=\left\lceil\frac{C}{R}\right\rceil. \]

If full-length prompts already saturate each replica and the scheduler minimizes mean first-token time by completing prefills in first-token-priority order, then

\[ \overline{\mathrm{TTFT}}_{\mathrm{burst}} \approx T_0(N)\frac{c_r+1}{2}, \qquad \mathrm{TTFT}_{\mathrm{last}} \approx T_0(N)c_r. \]

Long prompts are split into 2K-token chunks. GenZ includes active-path projection/MoE FLOPs, official stored bytes streamed per chunk, and architecture-specific attention arithmetic: dense MLA for Kimi, DSA index plus selected attention for GLM, KDA plus pooled DSA for GLM Flash, and the official 4×/128× compressed paths for V4 Flash. The resulting one-request TTFT centers at 72K/128K/256K are 6.9/16.6/54.2 s for Kimi, 4.3/7.4/15.7 s for GLM, 2.9/5.2/10.8 s for GLM Flash, and 4.4/8.6/20.2 s for V4 Flash. They are analytical centers, not measured end-to-end results.

\[ T_{\mathrm{complete},512} \approx \overline{\mathrm{TTFT}}_{\mathrm{burst}} +511\frac{\mathrm{TPOT}}{1000}. \]

7. Why full utilization is not an SLO

The graph's 100% point is a finite, closed batch. A continuously arriving service is different. A generic queueing approximation contains the factor

\[ W_q \propto \frac{\rho}{1-\rho}, \qquad \lim_{\rho\to1^-}W_q=\infty, \]

where \(\rho\) is offered utilization. Real long-prompt service times are highly variable, so the exact queue is not this simple; the divergence is the reason to preserve 25–50% operational headroom for prefills, misses, and burst absorption.

Planning guidance distinguishes latency targets from hard memory limits.

Uncertainty and exclusions

  • Not an A800 or full-model benchmark: A100 synthetic measurements ground the hardware envelope and GenZ supplies a roofline—not a kernel trace. The p10–p90 band samples several efficiency inputs but does not cover every A100→A800 topology error, routing skew, fusion failure, or framework gap. Core TPOT and cold TTFT can still be wrong by at least ±50%.
  • Steady decode and cold prefill are separated: the decode graphs assume requests have completed prefill. Mixing new 72K/128K/256K prefills into a full decode batch will cause TPOT spikes unless capacity is reserved.
  • Checkpoint bytes are measured, runtime bytes are modeled: official totals are 595.2 GB for Kimi, 755.6 GB for GLM, 328.3 GB for GLM Flash, and 159.6 GB for V4 Flash. Allocator alignment, duplicated metadata, kernels, and communication workspaces can raise HBM use.
  • Optimized MLA cache is assumed: the 576/512-value latent rows require a custom MLA serving kernel. Kimi's literal checked-in Transformers cache expands latent state into per-head K/V and would consume substantially more memory.
  • Sparse attention is a lower bound: Table 13 grounds its memory center, but the latent-width/direct-head adaptation is not a measured matrix-absorbed MLA kernel. No arbitrary launch constant is added; real launch and gather costs can only make the path slower.
  • DCP is not hidden inside TP: all growing latent/index history is replicated at DCP1. Explicit decode context parallelism could reduce per-rank history but adds distributed selection and attention communication and needs a separate case.
  • Pipeline topology and scheduling are assumed: Kimi and GLM use PP8×TP2, with stages 1–4 on one node and 5–8 on the other. The central scheduler searches microbatches up to \(\lceil C/P\rceil\), retaining at least eight request groups; real runtime batch queues can differ.
  • Stages must be time-balanced: equal layer counts need not mean equal work in a heterogeneous MoE model. The runtime should choose contiguous boundaries from measured stage time and weight footprint; the slowest stage sets pipeline cadence.
  • Host capacity is unbounded, bandwidth is not: system RAM cannot cause admission failure in this case. Exact caches must still remain NUMA-local to their consumer stage, and measured H2D plus assumed host-DRAM ceilings remain in every TPOT estimate.
  • Quality is assumed: the analysis does not prove that a fixed 1.56% selection policy preserves accuracy on these models and workloads.
  • Excluded latency: tokenization, API/network transit, detokenization, request logging, failures, retries, and multi-tenant isolation are not included.

Case A uses an advisory one-token-ahead oracle with 80% recall and 80% precision over the 40% miss set left after temporal reuse. Current-token landmark verification remains on the critical path. A100-SXM4 measurements ground the GenZ hardware envelope and ShadowKV transfer path; generated tables are consumed through pinned LLMServingSim commit a4053bc. No full frontier-model checkpoint was executed.
